one_liner: Header-only B+ tree implementing STL's map/set/multimap/multiset; beats libstdc++'s red-black tree at large n.
what_it_does: tlx::btree_map/btree_set/btree_multimap/btree_multiset are C++ template classes implementing the STL ordered-associative-container interface (iterators, find, insert, erase, operator[], lower_bound/upper_bound, comparison operators) using an in-memory B+ tree instead of a red-black tree. They take the same key/compare/allocator template parameters as std::map/std::set plus a traits type controlling node fanout, and add non-STL extras: exists(), insert2(), bulk_load(), get_stats(), and verify(). The public surface is close to, but not identical to, std::map/std::set.
how_it_is_fast: Leaf and inner nodes are sized by btree_default_traits to hold as many keys as fit in roughly a 256-byte block, so a comparison step touches one cache line instead of the one-key-per-node layout of a red-black tree. Leaves store keys and their associated data in two separate parallel arrays rather than an array of key/value pairs, and descent does an in-node search over a wide node instead of following per-key left/right/parent pointers. Net effect: fewer pointer-chasing cache misses per operation at large n, at the cost of more in-node comparisons per level.
when_to_use: Large (roughly >100k-1M+ element) in-memory ordered map/set/multiset/multimap of cheaply-comparable keys (e.g. integers) where insert, find and erase are all exercised and cache-miss-bound traversal dominates.
You want an STL-like drop-in-ish replacement for std::map/std::set without taking on SIMD or hugepage requirements.
You need sorted-order range queries (lower_bound/upper_bound/equal_range) alongside point lookups; B+ tree leaves are linked so range scans stay cheap.
You can vendor a small BSL-1.0 header (or the wider tlx repo) instead of a heavier dependency.
Your workload includes bulk-loading a pre-sorted range into an empty container (bulk_load()).
when_not_to_use: You rely on std::map's pointer/reference/iterator stability across insert/erase; tlx's B+ tree gives no such guarantee.
You need C++17/20 map features: emplace, try_emplace, insert_or_assign, extract, merge, or node_type/heterogeneous lookup; none appear in btree_map.hpp.
You need move construction/assignment on the container itself; only a copy constructor, copy assignment, and swap() are defined in the header I read.
Small containers (tens of elements or fewer); none of the record's benchmarks show a win below tens of thousands of items, and boost::flat_set/flat_map targets exactly that small-size regime.
You need erase(first,last) or lock-free/concurrent access; range-erase is unimplemented (only aborts under a debug-only macro) and no synchronization is documented or visible in the header.

integration.form: header-only (for the btree containers themselves; the wider tlx repo also builds a small static/shared libtlx for unrelated modules like digest/string helpers, but tlx/container/btree*.hpp are pure templates with no matching .cpp in LIBTLX_SOURCES)
integration.dependencies: none for normal insert/find/erase use (README states zero external dependencies; btree.hpp only includes <algorithm> <cassert> <cstddef> <functional> <iterator> <memory> <utility> and tlx/die/core.hpp). Caveat: verify() and the self_verify trait call tlx_die_unless() -> die_with_message(), which is declared in tlx/die/core.hpp but defined only in tlx/die/core.cpp, so using invariant verification requires linking libtlx or compiling that one file yourself.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 minimum. Root CMakeLists.txt auto-probes compiler flags, preferring -std=c++20 and falling back through c++17/c++14/c++11/c++0x. CI (.github/workflows/cmake.yml) builds with GCC 7.5, 9.3 (incl. -m32), 11, 13 and Clang 15 on macOS 13-15; requires CMake >= 3.7.
integration.platforms: x86-64 and 32-bit x86 on Linux, and macOS (Clang) are exercised in the GitHub Actions matrix I read; a Windows job exists in that same file but is commented out/disabled. README claims general portability ('smartphones, supercomputers, windows, etc.') and the README badge references a separate AppVeyor Windows build, which I did not open this session.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no locks or atomics are visible in tlx/container/btree.hpp. Treat it like std::map: concurrent writers need external synchronization.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same iterator/begin-end/find/insert/erase/operator[]/comparison-operator surface as std::map/std::set with the same Key/Compare/Allocator template parameter order, but missing emplace/try_emplace/insert_or_assign/extract/merge/node_type, no move constructor (only copy ctor/assign plus swap()), erase(first,last) not implemented, and no iterator/pointer stability guarantee across mutation (std::map guarantees this) — a mechanical typedef swap will not always compile or behave identically.

gotchas: verify()/self_verify require linking tlx/die/core.cpp (or libtlx) for die_with_message(); not fully header-only if you use invariant checking.
No move constructor or move-assignment on btree_map/btree_set — only copy constructor, copy assignment, and swap() are defined.
erase(first, last) is unimplemented: it only exists (and aborts) if TLX_BTREE_TODO is defined, otherwise the method is absent entirely.
No iterator/pointer stability guarantee across insert/erase, unlike std::map/std::set — don't hold iterators or pointers across mutations.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tlx::btree over fast-containers, S+/S-tree, or boost::container::flat_set/flat_map when the workload is genuinely dynamic (both insert and erase, not build-once-then-query) at large scale (roughly >100k-1M items) and you want a permissively licensed (BSL-1.0), dependency-free header with no SIMD/AVX/hugepage requirement; prefer S+/S-tree if the workload is static (bulk-built once, then read-only lower_bound queries), fast-containers if you can require SIMD+hugepages for its larger, more recently measured wins at 10M-element scale, or boost::flat_set/flat_map if containers stay small (roughly 2-128 elements).
verified_claims_summary: Evidence tier A: the author's own STX-btree/tlx speedtest (code public in tests/container/btree_speedtest.cpp) measured random-integer multiset insert-only, insert+find+erase, and find-only workloads at n from 125 to tens of millions against libstdc++'s std::multiset/std::multimap (red-black tree). Per the benchmark page (fetched this session): the 2007 run (g++ 4.1.2, -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer, Pentium 4 3.2GHz) showed the red-black tree taking almost 2x as long as a 32-slot B+ tree above roughly 1,024,000 items; the 2011/2013 reruns (gcc 4.4.5/4.5.0, Core i7 9xx, -O3 with -fomit-frame-pointer or -march=native) show the same divergence starting near 100,000 items. The input record additionally reports a 2019 in-repo results PDF (btree_speedtest_results.pdf, not opened by me this session) showing tlx::btree_multiset roughly 3x faster than std::multiset by n=2^26, with no hardware/compiler stated for that run.
status_note: Stale: last commit 2025-01-10 per the record, and the only open GitHub issue I found (#62) concerns the unrelated d_ary heap, not btree. BSL-1.0 licensed (unlike the GPL-3.0 predecessor stx-btree) and small enough to vendor as a handful of headers — copyable per the record's usability field.
